y-m-42-01.title: Can AB be calculated when BA cannot?
y-m-42-01.topic: Size condition for matrix product to be defined and multiplication order
y-m-42-01.goal: Know matrix product calculability depend on dimensions, not entry values; test claim ‘swap order’ with counterexample and generalize condition for both products.
y-m-42-01.material:
Only sizes of matrices A, B, C, D known; entry values unknown. (‘2×3’ read ‘2 by 3’, meaning 2 rows, 3 columns.)
- A: 2×3
- B: 3×2
- C: 2×2
- D: 3×3
Minjun say: ‘If you can calculate AB, you can also calculate BA by swapping order. Multiplication lets you swap order.’
y-m-42-01.thinking.0: Judge if product possible using sizes alone, without entry values
y-m-42-01.thinking.2: Generalize size condition for both products to be defined
y-m-42-01.prereq.0: Assume you already learn high-school Common Mathematics matrix unit (matrix meaning, addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication definition). ‘H2’ only task difficulty/support level, not a Ministry grade assignment.
y-m-42-01.prereq.1: Reading and writing matrix size m×n (m rows, n columns)
y-m-42-01.prereq.2: Condition for product of 2 matrices to be defined (columns in first equal rows in second), and product size
y-m-42-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all products whose calculability you can determine from sizes alone.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write each product as ‘size P · size Q’ and compare 2 middle numbers.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.hint.1: For products with different middle numbers, mark which differ; for matching ones, write result size too.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.a: Na choice matching columns of front matrix to rows of back matrix. Check which numbers you compared.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.b: Maybe you choose without comparing front columns (3) and back rows (2), thinking any pair can multiply.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.c: B get 2 columns and D get 3 rows. Maybe choice no match columns and rows of matrices being multiplied.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.d: Na choice comparing middle values in (2×3)(3×3).
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.e: Na choice comparing middle values in (3×3)(3×2).
y-m-42-01.s.s1.r.f: Maybe you think since AD works, DA works after swapping order. Compare D columns with A rows.
y-m-42-01.s.s1.explain: Product PQ defined only if columns of P equal rows of Q. CA (2×2 · 2×3), AD (2×3 · 3×3), DB (3×3 · 3×2) fit; result sizes 2×3, 2×3, 3×2. AC, BD, DA no fit because middle sizes differ.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.prompt: Use four matrices above to test Minjun claim ‘If AB calculable, BA also calculable.’ What you judge?
y-m-42-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write in words what kind of pair must exist to break claim ‘always.’
y-m-42-01.s.s2.hint.1: For products you find earlier like A and B, check one by one if swapped-order product defined too.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.o.a: Always true. Multiplication let you swap order.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.r.a: Na judgment wey carry familiar number multiplication order-swap to matrices as is.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.o.b: No. AD work but DA no work.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.r.b: You find counterexample by pairing defined product with swapped-order product.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.o.c: Sizes alone no tell; need entry values.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.r.c: Product calculability depend on sizes, no be entry values. Separate what need values and what sizes enough to know.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.o.d: Pairs like A and B both work, so claim true.
y-m-42-01.s.s2.r.d: You accept ‘always’ from one fitting example. What if you look for counterexample?
y-m-42-01.s.s2.explain: One counterexample break claim ‘always.’ AD works because (2×3)(3×3), but DA is (3×3)(2×3); middle 3 and 2 differ, so no. Product possibility depend on sizes, not entries.

y-m-42-01.s.s3.model.0: B must be n×m. Then AB is m×m, BA n×n; sizes must match before writing AB=BA, requiring m=n, meaning square matrix.
y-m-42-01.s.s3.model.1: For both products, B need n rows and m columns. To write AB=BA, products must have same size, so m and n must equal.
y-m-42-01.s.s3.model.2: B must have n rows, m columns. AB size m×m and BA size n×n, so AB=BA needs m=n.

y-m-42-03.title: Is it safe to cancel the same A from both sides?

y-m-42-03.s.s1.explain: Line 2 cancels A as if number; equal products do not guarantee cancellation for matrices. Thus line 4 “only E” is wrong. Line 3 correctly shows E is a solution, but not uniqueness. Line 1 also correct. [2 4 3 1]

y-m-42-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Haeun using examples why not cancel; give a condition allowing cancellation and X=E.

y-m-42-03.s.s3.model.0: X=[[3,0],[−1,1]] also gives AX=A, so canceling and keeping only E loses solutions. If A invertible, multiply inverse on left both sides to get X=E. [3 0 1 1]

y-m-42-03.s.s3.model.2: X=[[-1,2],[1,0]] also works. Only if A invertible can multiply both sides by inverse and get X=E. [1 2 1 0]
y-m-42-03.s.s3.modelNote.2: Answer with matrix written on one line
y-m-42-03.s.s3.model.3: X=[[3,2],[-1,0]] also gives AX=A. If A invertible, multiply both sides by A⁻¹ to conclude X=E. [3 2 1 0]
